text: The Cambrian explosion was a burst of new animal life in the seas, starting about 539 million years ago. Over roughly 20 million years, many of the main animal groups we know today appear in the [[fossil|fossil]] record for the first time. Before it, most living things were small and soft. After it, the seas held animals with shells, legs, spines, claws, guts and, for the first time, sharp eyes.

The word "explosion" sounds sudden, but it was only quick by the standards of Earth's history. Twenty million years is about 60 times longer than our own [[species|species]] has existed. Scientists still argue about what triggered it.

st.prompt: When Hallucigenia was first described in 1977, scientists got it badly wrong. What mistake did they make?

options.t: They drew it upside down, with spines as legs
They thought it was a plant
They mixed it up with a dinosaur

st.reveal: The first fossils showed a worm-like body with stiff spines on one side and floppy tubes on the other. Scientists thought it walked on the spines. Better fossils showed the tubes were legs and the spines were on its back for protection. Later work even found that the end they had called the head was its tail.

n.certNote: Everyone agrees that many animal groups appear in the fossil record during the Cambrian. Scientists debate how sudden it really was, how far back animals go before it, and what caused it.

Then show it to a friend upside down and see if they can work out which way up it goes. It's harder than it sounds, which is exactly the problem scientists faced.
myth: In the Cambrian explosion, animals appeared out of nowhere overnight.

It took tens of millions of years, and simpler animals already lived in the seas before it. What changed was that many animals grew hard parts, such as shells and spines, which fossilise more easily, so they suddenly show up much more in rocks.
facts: Anomalocaris, perhaps up to about half a metre long

sec.t:
In 1909, the American scientist Charles Walcott, head of the Smithsonian Institution, found a layer of rock high in the [[@rocky-mountains|Rocky Mountains]] of [[@canada|Canada]]. It was the Burgess Shale, and it had preserved soft-bodied animals in detail, down to guts and gills.

The animals were unlike anything alive today. Opabinia had five eyes on stalks and a long, flexible nose with a claw on the end. Anomalocaris, perhaps up to about half a metre long, had two spiny grabbing arms and a round mouth, and was one of the top hunters of its day. Pikaia, a small swimming worm-like animal, may be an early relative of all animals with backbones, including you.

In 1984, another rich site was found at Chengjiang in China, slightly older and just as detailed. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

There is no single answer. Many scientists think rising oxygen in the seas allowed bigger, more active animals. Others point to changes in ocean chemistry that made it easier to build shells.

Another idea focuses on [[@eyes-see|eyes]]. Once some animals could see, hunting became much more effective. Prey animals that grew armour, spines or speed survived better, and [[predator|predators]] improved in turn. Early animals such as [[@trilobites|trilobites]] had well-developed eyes. Most likely, several of these causes worked together.

Cambrian rocks are found in the [[@spiti|Spiti valley]] in [[@himachal|Himachal Pradesh]], high in the Himalaya. [[geologist|Geologists]] have collected trilobites there, especially around the Parahio valley.

These rocks formed on an ancient sea floor, long before India collided with Asia and pushed the Himalaya skyward. That means fossils of sea creatures now sit at heights of several kilometres, in one of the coldest, driest places in India. Reaching them can mean days of trekking at heights of around 4,000 m, and fossil hunters have to work fast in the short summer before snow returns. Fossils from Spiti also help geologists work out where ancient India sat on the globe, and which other lands it was close to back then.

text: The lowest dry land on Earth is the shore of the [[@dead-sea|Dead Sea]], a salt lake between Jordan, Israel and the West Bank. In the 2020s its surface lay more than 430 metres below sea level. That is deeper than the Eiffel Tower is tall.

And it is getting lower. The lake loses about a metre of depth each year. People take water from the Jordan River before it can reach the lake, and the hot sun dries out what is left. Every year, the lowest place you can walk on land moves a little further down.

st.prompt: Where is the lowest point on all of Earth's land surface, if you count ground hidden under ice?

options.t: At the bottom of the Dead Sea

st.reveal: Beneath the Denman Glacier in East Antarctica, a canyon in the rock dips about 3,500 metres below sea level. It is filled with ice, so nobody can stand there. The Dead Sea shore is the lowest place where you can walk in open air.

No fish or plants can survive there, but scientists have found tiny microbes, such as some bacteria and algae, living in the salty water and in springs on the sea floor.

sec.t:
The Dead Sea sits in a long crack in Earth's crust called the Jordan Rift Valley. Two pieces of crust are sliding past each other here, and the land between them has dropped. It is part of the same system that runs south into Africa, where the [[@great-rift-valley|Great Rift Valley]] is slowly splitting the continent.

Water flows in, but no river flows out. The only way out is up, as water [[evaporation|evaporates]] in the desert heat. The salt is left behind, so the lake has grown saltier for thousands of years. Today it is almost 10 times saltier than the ocean. In 1947, a young shepherd exploring caves near the lake's north-west shore found ancient writings in clay jars. These Dead Sea Scrolls are more than 2,000 years old, and the dry desert air helped them survive.

As the water falls, it leaves behind dry land with salt hidden underground. Fresh rainwater and groundwater seep in and [[dissolve|dissolve]] that salt, leaving empty spaces. The ground above then collapses. Thousands of [[@sinkholes|sinkholes]] have opened along the shore since the 1980s, swallowing roads, fields and even buildings.

The ruins of old beach resorts now sit far from the water's edge. Some places where people once swam are now hundreds of metres from the lake.

sec.h: The lowest spots on other continents
sec.t:
Every continent has its own low point. In the United States, Badwater Basin in Death Valley lies 86 metres (282 feet) below sea level. A sign on a nearby cliff marks where sea level would be, high above visitors' heads. Death Valley is also one of the hottest places on Earth. Lake Assal in Djibouti, Africa's lowest point, sits about 155 metres down.

India's lowest point is Kuttanad in Kerala. Its rice fields lie up to about 2 metres below sea level, protected by mud walls, and farmers pump water out to plant their [[@rice|rice]].

If you could peel away the ice, Antarctica would beat them all. In 2019, scientists mapping the rock beneath the ice found a canyon under the Denman Glacier about 3,500 metres below sea level. It is packed with ice, so no one can visit.

Under water, things get far deeper. The bottom of the Mariana Trench in the Pacific is nearly 11,000 metres below the surface. And the strangest part? If you dropped Mount Everest into it, its peak would still be more than 2 kilometres underwater, as you'll see in the story of the [[@ocean-deepest|deepest part of the ocean]].

text: A heatwave is a spell of days that are much hotter than normal for a place and time of year. Heatwaves have always happened. What has changed is how often they come and how hot they get.

The main reason is [[@climate-change|climate change]]. Burning coal, oil and gas adds [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]] to the air, which traps extra heat. By the 2010s, Earth's average temperature had risen by about 1.1 °C since the late 1800s, according to the IPCC, the United Nations' panel of [[climate|climate]] scientists. That sounds small. But when the whole curve of temperatures shifts upwards, the hottest days get hotter and far more common.
Other things add to it. Cities trap heat, dry soil warms faster, and natural patterns like [[@el-nino|El Niño]] can push some years higher still.

st.prompt: On a hot night, a big city stays warmer than the countryside around it. Why?

options.t: Concrete and roads soak up heat by day and give it off at night
Cities are closer to the Sun
City lights give off most of the extra heat

st.reveal: Roads, roofs and walls absorb sunlight all day and release it slowly after dark. Cities also have fewer trees and less water to cool the air. This is called the urban heat island effect, and it can make city nights several degrees warmer.

d.try: On a sunny day, place two identical thermometers or two cups of water in the sun, one on a dark surface and one on a white cloth. After an hour, ask an adult to help you compare the readings. This is why some cities paint roofs white to keep homes cooler.
myth: A few hot summers prove nothing, because the weather has always gone up and down.

Weather does vary, but scientists look at decades of records worldwide. Hot extremes have become more frequent and more intense since the 1950s, and the IPCC says human-caused warming is the main driver.
facts: at least 40 °C and well above normal, or 45 °C or more

sec.h: How a small shift makes a big difference
sec.t:
Picture a year's daily temperatures as a hill-shaped graph. Most days sit in the middle, and very hot days are rare, out in the thin tail on the right. Now nudge the whole hill one step to the right. The middle barely looks different, but the tail of extreme heat grows much fatter. Days that used to be rare become regular, and new records become possible.

Scientists can now test single events. Groups such as World Weather Attribution compare the real world with computer models of a world without human warming. For many recent heatwaves, they found the heat would have been almost impossible without climate change.

Your body stays near 37 °C by [[@sweat|sweating]]. As sweat evaporates, it carries heat away from the skin. But in very humid air, sweat can't evaporate well, so you can't cool down properly. That is why hot, sticky weather can be more dangerous than dry heat at the same temperature.

Doctors warn that heatstroke can be deadly. Older people, babies, outdoor workers and people without cool homes face the most danger. On very hot days, drinking water often, staying in shade and resting in the hottest hours all help. If you feel dizzy or sick in the heat, tell an adult straight away.

In 2010, a severe heatwave struck [[@ahmedabad|Ahmedabad]] and many people died. In 2013, the city launched a heat action plan, one of the first in South Asia. It sends out early warnings, keeps parks and water points open, trains health workers and helps people paint roofs white or light colours to reflect sunlight. Many other Indian cities and states now have similar plans.

In the USA, cities like Phoenix have opened cooling centres and planted [[@what-if-no-trees|shade trees]]. [[@air-conditioning|Air conditioning]] saves lives, but it also uses a lot of electricity and pumps heat outdoors, so planners are also looking at trees, water and smarter buildings to keep streets cooler.

text: On 24 October 1946, a rocket blasted off from White Sands in the New Mexico desert in the USA. It was a V-2, a German war rocket captured at the end of the Second World War. Tucked inside was a 35 mm movie camera, set to snap a frame every second and a half.

The rocket climbed to about 105 km, roughly twelve times higher than Mount Everest. Then it fell back and smashed into the sand. The camera broke, but the film was safe inside a steel case. When the scientists developed it, they saw grainy black-and-white pictures of the curved Earth under a black sky. Nobody had ever seen that before. Each frame covered a patch of the American Southwest bigger than many Indian states, all in one glance.

st.prompt: In 1946 a rocket camera took the first photos from space, then the rocket crashed into the ground. How did the film survive?

options.t: It was packed inside a steel case
It floated down on a parachute of its own
The photos were sent back by radio

st.reveal: The camera itself was smashed to bits when the rocket hit the desert. But the film sat inside a tough steel cassette, and scientists dug it out of the wreck and developed it.

d.try: Look at a small object, like a coin, from your nose, then from across the room, then from the far end of a corridor. Notice the point where you stop seeing any detail. That is roughly what happened to Earth in photos as spacecraft flew farther and farther away.
myth: The first photo of Earth from space was taken by an astronaut.
The first ones were taken in 1946 by an automatic camera on an uncrewed rocket. No human went to space until Yuri Gagarin in 1961.
facts: a captured German V-2, launched from New Mexico, USA

sec.t:
The pictures were blurry, and they showed only clouds and desert. But people who were there later remembered the scientists jumping up and down like children when they saw them. Newspapers and magazines printed them as the view a space traveller would see.

Over the next few years, more rocket cameras flew. In 1954, a small rocket called an Aerobee caught a huge storm swirling over Texas. Weather forecasters were stunned. From the ground, they had seen only bits of the storm. From above, it was one giant spiral. That idea would later lead to [[@weather-satellites|weather satellites]], which now watch every [[cyclone|cyclone]] on Earth.

On 7 December 1972, the crew of Apollo 17 took a photo of the whole Earth, fully lit, from about 29,000 km away. The Sun was behind them, so there were no shadows. You can see Africa, the Arabian [[peninsula|peninsula]] and the swirling clouds over Antarctica. It became known as the Blue Marble.

For decades it was the best-known photo of the whole round Earth taken by a person's own hands. Most later full-Earth images come from robot spacecraft, and many are stitched together from smaller pictures.

India has taken its own. In November 2013, a camera on ISRO's Mangalyaan, heading for Mars, snapped Earth with the Indian [[subcontinent|subcontinent]] clearly visible.

On 14 February 1990, the spacecraft [[@voyager|Voyager 1]] turned its camera back towards home from about 6 billion km away. Earth showed up as a tiny speck, smaller than a single [[pixel|pixel]], caught in a streak of scattered sunlight. The [[astronomer|astronomer]] Carl Sagan called it the Pale Blue Dot.

So the story goes from a grainy desert snapshot to a dot almost too small to see. A photo taken from a Mumbai rooftop can show more detail of a cricket match than the Voyager picture shows of the whole planet. And Voyager is still out there, now more than 25 billion km away (2026), carrying a golden record of Earth's sounds in case anyone ever finds it.

text: In 1963, only about 417 pairs of bald eagles were nesting in the lower 48 states of the USA. The cause was a [[pesticide|pesticide]] called DDT, sprayed on farms and towns to kill insects. It washed into rivers, built up in fish, and then in the eagles that ate them. It made their eggshells so thin that they cracked when the parents sat on them.

The USA banned DDT in 1972 and protected the birds by law. Slowly, the eagles came back. In 2007 they were taken off the [[endangered|endangered]] list. A government survey published in 2021 estimated more than 3 lakh (300,000) bald eagles in the lower 48 states.

st.reveal: The pesticide DDT washed into rivers, built up in fish and then in eagles. It made their eggshells too thin to hold the parent's weight.

d.try: Show how a poison piles up with beads or dried peas. Fill ten small cups with plain beads and drop one red bead into each cup. These are the fish. Now let the "eagle" tip all ten cups into one bowl and count the red beads it has collected.
myth: Benjamin Franklin wanted the turkey to be the national bird of the USA.
Franklin never made that proposal. In a private letter to his daughter he grumbled about the eagle's habits and called the turkey a more respectable bird, and the story grew from there.
facts: about 417 nesting pairs (1963, lower 48 US states)

sec.t:
DDT does not break down easily. A fish swallows a tiny amount with its food, and the chemical stays in its fat. An eagle eats hundreds of fish, so it collects their DDT too. Scientists call this [[biomagnification|biomagnification]]: a poison becomes more concentrated at each step up a [[foodchain|food chain]].

In female eagles, the chemical upset the way their bodies built eggshells. The eggs looked normal but were too thin to survive being sat on. Ospreys, brown pelicans and [[@sky-peregrine|peregrine falcons]] suffered in the same way. In 1962 the scientist and writer Rachel Carson warned about pesticides in her book *Silent Spring*. It helped turn many Americans against DDT.

India has its own version of this story. From the 1990s, India's [[@vultures-india|vultures]] began dying in huge numbers, and more than 95 per cent of some [[species|species]] vanished. Scientists traced the deaths to diclofenac, a painkiller given to cattle. Vultures that fed on dead cattle suffered kidney failure. India banned diclofenac for animals in 2006, and the fall has slowed.

{{story:bison-return}}

The bald eagle has been on the [[@american-revolution|Great Seal of the United States]] since 1782. In December 2024 a new law made it the official national bird. Not everyone has liked it. In a 1784 letter, Benjamin Franklin called it a bird of "bad moral character", because it often steals fish from other birds.

It isn't bald, either. The name comes from an old English word for white, describing the white head. Young eagles are brown all over and only get their white heads at about four or five years old. India chose a very different bird for its [[@national-symbols|national symbols]]: the colourful peacock.

Banning DDT was only the start. In 1973 the USA passed the Endangered Species Act, which made it illegal to harm bald eagles or their nests. [[biologist|Biologists]] also moved young eagles from places with many birds to places with none, raising them on tall platforms until they could fly. Cleaner rivers meant healthier fish, and healthier fish meant healthier eagles.

By the 1990s the numbers were climbing fast. Eagles still face dangers. Some swallow lead fragments from hunters' bullets in the [[carcass|carcasses]] they scavenge, and lead is a poison. Others are hit by cars or fly into power lines. Scientists keep counting nests, because the eagle's story showed how quickly a top hunter can warn us that something is wrong further down the chain.

Bald eagles mostly eat fish, which they snatch from the water with their feet. A pair often uses the same nest for many years and adds new sticks every season. One famous nest in St Petersburg, Florida, was about 2.9 m wide and 6 m deep. It was thought to weigh more than 2 tonnes, about as much as a large car.

With wings up to about 2.3 m across, an eagle can [[@gliders|soar for hours on rising warm air]], a trick explained in [[@how-birds-fly|how birds fly]]. Like the [[@bison-return|American bison]], it shows that a species can recover when people remove the danger and give it room.

text: Hornbills are big forest birds with huge curved beaks, many topped by a hollow helmet called a casque. About 60 kinds live in Africa and Asia, and 9 in India. The largest Indian one, the great hornbill, can have wings 1.5 metres across. When it flies overhead, the air rushing through its feathers makes a loud whooshing sound, like a steam engine puffing.

They are special for three big reasons. They have one of the strangest nesting habits of any bird. They plant forests by spreading seeds. And for many communities in northeast India and the [[@western-ghats|Western Ghats]], they are deeply woven into culture.

st.prompt: While she is sealed in the nest, what happens to the mother great hornbill's feathers?

options.t: She sheds her flight feathers and can't fly

st.reveal: Safe inside the tree, the female moults her flight feathers and grows new ones. For weeks she depends completely on the male, who flies back again and again with fruit, and sometimes lizards or insects, for her and the chick.

d.try: Hornbills spread seeds by eating fruit and dropping the seeds far away. Collect a few seeds from fruit you eat, such as papaya or tomato, wash them, and plant them in a pot of soil. Keep it moist and see how many sprout in two weeks. In a forest, the seeds a hornbill drops get the same chance to grow.
myth: A hornbill's huge beak and the "helmet" on top must be very heavy.

The casque, the helmet-like part on top, is mostly hollow inside, with thin walls and a light honeycomb of bone. It may help the call sound louder. Only the helmeted hornbill of South-East Asia has a solid casque.
facts: a hole in a tall tree, sealed with mud and droppings

sec.t:
When it's time to nest, a pair of great hornbills finds a hole high up in an old tree. The female climbs inside. Then, using mud, food and her own droppings, she seals the entrance, leaving only a narrow slit. The male passes her food through this gap, sometimes coughing up dozens of figs one after another.

She stays inside for three months or more, lays her eggs and raises her chick. While she's there, she sheds her flight feathers and grows new ones. The wall keeps out snakes, monkeys and other egg thieves. If anything happens to the male, the family is in danger, which is why every nesting male matters.

Great hornbill pairs often stay together for years, and many return to the same nest tree season after season. Big old trees with holes wide enough are rare, so losing one can leave a pair with nowhere to breed.

For many communities in India's [[@northeast-india|northeast]], the hornbill is a symbol of courage and beauty. Naga dancers wear its feathers, and Nagaland names its biggest yearly celebration the Hornbill Festival, held from 1 to 10 December. It began in 2000 and is now held at Kisama, a heritage village near Kohima, where dancers, cooks and craftspeople from all the major Naga tribes gather. Hunting for beaks and feathers once took a heavy toll. In Arunachal Pradesh, the Nyishi people now often wear headgear with beaks made of fibreglass instead of real ones.

In 2011, the Nature Conservation Foundation and the forest department began a nest adoption programme around Pakke Tiger Reserve. Members of the Nyishi community, some of them former hunters, now guard nest trees. People anywhere can pay to "adopt" a nest, and the money supports the guardians. The number of known nests protected has grown year by year.

Great hornbills live in the forests of the Western Ghats, the Himalayan foothills and the northeast. The great hornbill is the state bird of both Kerala and Arunachal Pradesh. In Kerala, it can be spotted in places like the Athirappilly forests. The smaller Indian grey hornbill is much easier to find. It even lives in parks in cities such as Delhi, where you may hear its squeaky call or see it flapping and gliding between trees.

Across the sea in Africa, ground hornbills walk on the [[savanna|savanna]] hunting insects and snakes, and red-billed hornbills hop around camps looking for scraps. Zazu, the fussy adviser in Disney's *The Lion King*, is one of these.

text: A weather balloon carries a small box of instruments, called a radiosonde, up through the [[atmosphere|atmosphere]]. As it rises, the box measures temperature, [[humidity|humidity]] and air pressure, and radios the numbers back to the ground every second or two. By tracking where the balloon drifts, forecasters also learn how fast and in which direction the wind is blowing at every height.

These readings feed the [[@supercomputers|computer models]] that make [[@weather-forecasts|weather forecasts]]. Every day at the same two moments, midnight and noon on the clock used by scientists, balloons go up from about 900 sites around the world. Together they give a snapshot of the whole sky at once.

st.prompt: As a weather balloon rises higher and higher, what happens to it?

options.t: It swells up until it bursts
It shrinks because the air is cold
It floats at one height for weeks

st.reveal: The higher it goes, the less air is pressing on the outside of the balloon. The gas inside pushes outwards and the rubber stretches, until the balloon is many times wider than at launch and pops. A small parachute brings the instruments down.

d.try: Blow up a balloon only a little and tie it. Put it in the fridge for twenty minutes and watch it shrink, then leave it in a warm, sunny spot and watch it swell. Air takes up more space when it is warm or when there is less air pressing on it, which is exactly what happens to a weather balloon as it rises.
myth: Satellites have made weather balloons unnecessary.

Satellites watch the whole planet, but they see the air from above. Balloons pass straight through it and measure each layer directly. Forecasters still use both, and the balloon readings help check and correct what satellites see.
facts: temperature, humidity, air pressure and wind

sec.h: A two-hour trip to the edge of space
How balloons found a new layer of sky
sec.t:
In the 1890s, a French scientist named Léon Teisserenc de Bort began sending up hundreds of unmanned balloons with instruments. He expected the air to keep getting colder the higher it went. Instead, his records showed that above about 11 km, the temperature stopped falling.

In 1902 he announced that the atmosphere has layers. The lowest, where all our weather happens, is now called the troposphere. The calmer layer above is the stratosphere. Today's balloons cross from one to the other on every flight. The boundary between them is not fixed. It sits higher over the hot tropics, around 16–17 km above places like Chennai, and lower near the poles, which balloon records helped scientists discover.

sec.h: From the monsoon to the jet stream
sec.t:
The India Meteorological Department launches weather balloons from stations across the country. Their readings help track the [[@monsoon|monsoon]] winds as they push north each summer, and follow [[@cyclones-india|cyclones forming over the Bay of Bengal]] and the Arabian Sea.

Balloons also measure the [[@jet-streams|jet streams]], fast rivers of wind about 10 km up. Modern radiosondes work out their position using [[@gps-how|satellite navigation]], so forecasters can calculate wind speeds very precisely as the balloon is blown along. Pilots care about these numbers too. A plane flying east across the United States with a strong jet stream behind it can arrive well ahead of schedule, while one flying west into it burns extra fuel.

sec.h: A balloon mistaken for a flying saucer
sec.t:
In 1947, a rancher near Roswell, New Mexico, found strange wreckage of foil, rubber and sticks. Rumours spread that it came from an alien spacecraft. In 1994, a report by the US Air Force concluded the debris came from Project Mogul, a secret string of balloons built to listen for distant nuclear tests.

Ordinary weather balloons are still sometimes reported as UFOs, especially at sunset, when a balloon high in the sky catches sunlight long after the ground below has gone dark.

text: [[sustainable|Sustainable]] fishing means catching fish in a way that leaves enough behind to breed, so there will be just as many fish next year and the year after. It's a bit like a bank account. Spend only the interest and the money lasts for ever. Spend the savings and one day it's gone.

To do this, fishers and governments set limits on how many fish can be caught, how big they must be and when and where fishing is allowed. They also try to protect other sea animals, and the seabed itself, from being harmed by nets and lines.
Billions of people eat fish, and millions earn their living from it, from small boats in [[@kerala|Kerala]] to giant trawlers in the North Atlantic. Keeping the oceans full matters to all of them.

st.prompt: India bans most fishing by mechanised boats for about two months each year. Why then?

options.t: It's when many fish breed, so young fish get a chance to grow

sec.t:
The Grand Banks, off Newfoundland in [[@canada|Canada]], were once among the richest fishing grounds on Earth. Early European sailors reported cod so thick that they could almost scoop them up in baskets.

In the 20th century, huge factory trawlers began catching cod around the clock. Catches soared, then collapsed. By 1992, the cod had almost disappeared. Canada banned cod fishing there, and tens of thousands of people lost their jobs overnight.

Scientists expected the cod to bounce back within a few years. More than three decades later, they still haven't fully recovered. Once a fish population falls too low, the whole [[ecosystem|ecosystem]] can change around it.

Nets don't choose. Fishing gear often traps animals nobody wanted, such as young fish, turtles, dolphins, seabirds and sharks. This is called bycatch. Shrimp and prawn trawling is especially wasteful, because the nets have small holes and scoop up almost everything.

Some fixes are simple. Nets with bigger holes let young fish escape. Trawl nets can be fitted with a turtle excluder device, a metal grid with a flap that lets [[@sea-turtles|sea turtles]] push their way out. Long fishing lines can be set at night, when seabirds aren't diving for bait.

Bottom trawling, dragging heavy nets across the seabed, can also wreck coral and sponge gardens that took centuries to grow.

Many countries close fishing during breeding seasons. In India, mechanised boats stop fishing for 61 days each year, during the [[monsoon|monsoon]] months. On the east coast the ban runs from mid-April to mid-June, and on the west coast from June to July.

Rules can bring fish back. Atlantic bluefin tuna, a favourite for [[@sushi|sushi]], was heavily overfished. After years of strict catch limits, its numbers rose, and in 2021 the IUCN, which tracks [[endangered|endangered]] [[species|species]], moved it out of the "endangered" group.

Some fish carry labels, like the blue tick of the Marine Stewardship Council, which certify they come from well-managed fisheries. Eating a wider range of local fish, not just a few famous kinds, also spreads the pressure. Asking "where was this caught?" is a small question that fishers and shopkeepers increasingly expect to hear.

Hyenas do scavenge too, and they are very good at it, cracking bones that other animals leave behind. But the image of a hyena as a cowardly thief is mostly wrong.
India's own hyena, the striped hyena, is different. It is shy, mostly solitary and does live mainly by scavenging, along with insects, fruit and small animals.

sec.t:
A spotted hyena's jaws are among the strongest of any [[mammal|mammal]] for its size. Its big back teeth and huge jaw muscles can crunch through a giraffe's leg bone. It can digest bone, hoof and even horn, leaving very little behind. That's why its droppings often turn chalky white, packed with calcium from all the bone.

Hyenas also have tough stomachs. They can eat meat that would make most animals sick. By clearing away [[carcass|carcasses]], they help keep disease down on the [[savanna|savanna]], much like [[@vultures-india|vultures]] do in India.

Spotted hyenas live in clans that can number up to about 80, though they often hunt in smaller groups. Females are larger than males and in charge. The top female rules, her cubs rank next, and males that join from other clans sit at the bottom.

Their famous "laugh" is not about anything funny. It is a high giggle hyenas make when they are excited, frustrated or being pushed away from food by a stronger hyena. Scientists have found that the sound carries information about the hyena's age and rank. Hyenas also whoop, a loud call that can be heard several kilometres away, to call clan members.

The striped hyena lives across dry parts of India, from the scrublands of Rajasthan and Gujarat to the Deccan. It is smaller than the spotted hyena, with grey fur, black stripes and a shaggy mane along its back that stands up when it is frightened, making it look bigger.

It mostly comes out at night, travelling long distances alone in search of carcasses. Near villages it may eat livestock remains and rubbish. People rarely see it, and old stories made it a creature of fear, though it almost never attacks humans.

It shares some of the same scrublands as India's [[@wolves-india|wolves]], and both struggle as grasslands are ploughed up or built over.

In the old walled city of Harar, in [[@ethiopia|Ethiopia]], hyenas have wandered the streets at night for centuries. People there leave out scraps, and for decades some families have fed wild hyenas by hand after dark, calling them by name.

The hyenas help clean the city of food waste, and many residents see them as good neighbours. The smallest hyena of all, the aardwolf, would not be interested in those scraps. It eats almost nothing but termites, lapping up many thousands of them a night with a long, sticky tongue.

text: Sunlight looks white, but it is a mix of all the colours of the [[@rainbow-how|rainbow]]. As it passes through the air, the tiny gas [[molecule|molecules]] bump blue light off in every direction much more than red light. This is called *scattering*.

At noon, the Sun is high and its light takes a short path through the air. Plenty of blue gets scattered across the sky, which is why the [[@sky-blue|daytime sky is blue]]. At sunset, the Sun is low and its light has to travel sideways through dozens of times more air. By the time it reaches you, most of the blue and green have been scattered away. What's left is orange and red.

sec.h: A long road through the air
sec.t:
The layer of air around Earth is thin, a bit like the skin on an apple. Straight up, sunlight crosses it quickly. Near the horizon, the light skims through the layer at a low angle, the way a cricket ball skids a long way along the ground after a low throw.

Along that long road, blue light is scattered out of the beam again and again. Red light, with its longer waves, mostly keeps going. The Sun itself turns orange, and any clouds overhead are lit from below in pink, gold and red. Lord Rayleigh, a British scientist, worked out the maths of this scattering in 1871.

On [[@mars-sky|Mars]], everything is flipped. In 2015, NASA's [[@tech-robots-space|Curiosity rover]] photographed the Sun setting over a [[crater|crater]]. The sky near the Sun glowed a cool blue. Mars has very thin air but lots of fine dust, and that dust happens to scatter blue light forwards, in the direction the sunlight is already moving.

Dust and smoke near the ground often make sunsets look dull and muddy rather than bright. In winter, Delhi's hazy evenings often show a pale orange Sun without much colour around it. Clearer air with some high clouds tends to give the best displays, like the famous evenings over the sea at [[@kanyakumari|Kanyakumari]] or the red cliffs of the [[@grand-canyon|Grand Canyon]] in [[@grand-canyon-state|Arizona]].

An old English rhyme says "Red sky at night, shepherd's delight". Over much of Europe and the USA, weather usually travels from west to east. There, a glowing sunset can mean clear, dry air lies to the west and is heading your way. It's a rule of thumb, though, not a forecast.

Near the horizon, the air bends sunlight a little, the same way water bends a straw in a glass. This bending lifts the image of the [[@sun-what|Sun]] slightly, so you can still see it for a couple of minutes after it has dipped below the horizon. It also squashes the Sun into a flattened oval. The Sun you watch setting is, for a few moments, already gone.

text: Sunglasses protect your eyes in two ways. First, good lenses block ultraviolet (UV) light, invisible rays from the Sun that can damage the eye over time. Second, tinted lenses cut down bright visible light and glare, so you can see comfortably without squinting.

The most important part is invisible. A label saying "UV400" or "100% UV protection" means the lenses stop almost all [[ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] light. The colour and darkness of the lens only change how bright things look, not how much UV gets through.

sec.t:
Sunlight contains light of many [[wavelength|wavelengths]]. We see only part of it, the colours of the rainbow. Just beyond violet lies ultraviolet light, which our eyes cannot see. UV is what causes [[@sunburn-sunscreen|sunburn]] on skin.

Eyes can get sunburnt too. Too much UV in one day can burn the clear front surface of the eye, causing pain, tears and a gritty feeling. Skiers and mountaineers call this snow blindness, because snow reflects so much sunlight back up. Over many years, UV also raises the risk of cataracts, a clouding of the eye's lens that is one of the main causes of poor sight in older people.

sec.h: The danger of cheap dark lenses

sec.t:
Sunlight bounces off flat surfaces like water, wet roads and car bonnets. Much of that reflected light becomes polarised, meaning its waves vibrate mostly in one direction, side to side. That is the dazzling glare that makes you squint.

Polarised lenses contain a filter with millions of tiny lined-up [[molecule|molecules]], like the slats of a fence. They block light waves vibrating side to side and let through those moving up and down. Glare disappears, and you can often see fish under the surface of a pond. In the 1930s, American inventor Edwin Land made polarising filters cheap enough for sunglasses, and fishers and drivers loved them.

People protected their eyes from glare long before modern lenses. Inuit and other Arctic peoples carved goggles with thin slits from bone, wood or [[antler|antler]]. The slits let in only a sliver of light, enough to see but not enough to be blinded by the snow. Some found by [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] are around 2,000 years old.

Modern sunglasses became popular in the USA after 1929, when a businessman named Sam Foster began selling cheap ones on the beach at Atlantic City. Film stars wore them, and soon everyone wanted a pair. During the 1930s, American pilots got special green-tinted glasses for flying high in bright sunshine, a style still known as aviators.

UV is strongest at high altitudes, on snow, near water and around noon. In India's summer, and in places like Ladakh where the air is thin, it can be very strong indeed. So sunglasses with a UV400 label are a good idea outdoors, along with a hat. But no sunglasses are safe for staring at the Sun. During an [[@eclipses|eclipse]], only special [[eclipse|eclipse]] glasses that block almost all sunlight will do. And the reason less UV reaches the ground in the first place is a thin shield of gas high above us, the [[@ozone-layer|ozone layer]].

text: The International Mathematical Olympiad, or IMO, is the world's top maths competition for school students. Each year, every country can send a team of up to six students who are younger than 20 and not yet at university.

The contest takes two days. Each day students get three problems and four and a half hours to solve them. The questions need no advanced maths beyond school, but they are extremely tricky, and answers must be written as full proofs, step-by-step arguments that leave no gaps. Each problem is worth 7 points, so a perfect score is 42.

sec.t:
The first IMO was held in Romania in 1959, with seven countries from Eastern Europe. It grew slowly at first, then quickly. Today more than 100 countries take part, and a different country hosts it each year.

India first sent a team in 1989. Seven years later, in 1996, India hosted the IMO in Mumbai. The United States has taken part since 1974 and has topped the medal table several times.

Olympiad problems are closer to [[@puzzles-logic|logic puzzles]] than to homework. A problem might ask you to prove that some pattern always happens, or to find every whole number that fits a strange rule. Most fall into four areas: [[@algebra|algebra]], number theory (the study of whole numbers), [[@geometry-everyday|geometry]] and combinatorics (clever counting).

A strong student might spend two hours staring at one problem before spotting the key idea. Then the solution can fit on half a page.

sec.h: A taste of the very first contest
sec.t:
The first problem at the 1959 IMO asked students to prove that the fraction (21n + 4) ÷ (14n + 3) can never be simplified, whatever whole number n is. Trying examples shows it works for n = 1, 2 and 3, but examples are not a proof.

The trick is short. Three lots of the bottom number minus two lots of the top number always equals exactly 1. Any number that divided both top and bottom would also have to divide 1. So nothing bigger than 1 can, and the fraction never simplifies. That one neat idea is the whole solution, which is typical of olympiad maths.

Maths is not the only subject with olympiads. There are international contests in physics, chemistry, biology, astronomy and computer programming too, and India sends teams to all of them.

Medals go to no more than half of all contestants. They are split roughly in the ratio of one gold to two silvers to three bronzes. Students who don't win a medal but solve one problem perfectly get an honourable mention.

Many medallists become research mathematicians. Terence Tao, who grew up in [[@australia|Australia]], won gold at 13. Maryam Mirzakhani of Iran won golds in 1994 and 1995 and later became the first woman to win the [[@indian-mathematicians-modern|Fields Medal]], in 2014. Her story is one of many in the history of [[@women-maths|women in maths]]. Plenty of other contestants go on to work in computing, science, engineering or medicine.

text: When you whack your "funny bone", you're actually hitting your ulnar nerve. This nerve runs from your neck down to your hand. At the elbow, it passes through a shallow groove on the inner side, with only skin and a thin layer of fat on top. There's no muscle to cushion it.

So a knock squashes the nerve against hard bone. That sends a sudden burst of signals racing to your brain. Your brain reads them as a strange mix of sharp pain, electric buzz and pins and needles, shooting down into your little finger. It isn't funny at all, but it usually wears off within a minute.

sec.t:
[[nerve|Nerves]] are like electric cables. Most of them run deep inside your body, wrapped in muscle and fat for protection. The ulnar nerve is unlucky. For a few centimetres at the elbow, it lies just under the skin in a groove called the cubital tunnel.

You can feel the spot yourself. Find the bony bump on the inner side of your elbow, then the point of your elbow. The groove between them is where the nerve runs. Doctors sometimes tap it gently to test whether the nerve is working.

Your brain is good at many things, but it doesn't always know where a signal started. When the ulnar nerve is hit at the elbow, the brain gets a message from a cable that normally carries feeling from your little finger and part of your ring finger.

So the brain blames those fingers. You feel tingling there, even though nothing touched them. Doctors call this referred sensation. It is the same kind of confusion that makes [[@body-brain-freeze|brain freeze]] hurt in your forehead when the cold is really in your mouth.

Nobody knows exactly where the name "funny bone" came from. It has been used in English since at least the 1800s. One popular explanation is a pun. The long bone in your upper arm is called the humerus, which sounds like "humorous". Hit near the end of the humerus, and you get the "humorous bone".

Others say it's just because the feeling is so odd, or "funny peculiar" rather than "funny ha-ha". Either way, people find the name funnier than the feeling.

A quick bump is harmless. But some people get tingling in their little finger even without bumping anything. That can happen if the nerve is squeezed for a long time, for example by leaning on your elbows or sleeping with arms bent tight. Long phone calls with a bent elbow can do it too.

If tingling or weakness in the hand keeps coming back, it's worth telling a parent or doctor. Usually small changes, like keeping your elbows straighter, sort it out.

Your body has other quick-fire wiring that works without you thinking. Tap just below the kneecap and your leg kicks before your brain even knows, thanks to the [[@reflexes|reflexes]] built into your spinal cord.

text: A feeling, or emotion, is your brain's quick judgement about what is happening and what it means for you. When something matters, your brain sends signals through your body. Your heart may race, [[@body-belly-sounds|your face may change]], your stomach may flutter. At the same time, you notice an inner sense of fear, joy, anger or sadness.

Feelings help you act quickly. Fear gets you ready to escape. Disgust keeps you away from rotten food. Joy makes you want to do good things again. Sadness can slow you down and bring others to comfort you. Scientists still argue about exactly how the brain makes feelings, but they agree that emotions involve the brain and body working together.

sec.t:
There's no single feelings centre in the [[@brain-works|brain]]. Many parts work together. Deep inside sit two almond-shaped bundles called the [[amygdala|amygdala]]. They help spot danger very quickly, sometimes before you're even aware of it. That's why you can jump at a rope on the ground before you realise it isn't a snake.

The front of the brain, behind your forehead, helps you understand your feelings and decide what to do with them. In children and teenagers, this part is still growing. Strong feelings can arrive quickly, while the ability to calm them develops over years.

People thought hard about emotions long before modern science. The Natya Shastra, an ancient Indian text on drama usually credited to the sage Bharata, describes rasas, the flavours of feeling an audience tastes during a performance. It listed eight, and later writers added a ninth, peace. Together they're called the navarasa.

Dancers in [[@indian-classical-dance|Indian classical dance]] forms like [[@bharatanatyam|Bharatanatyam]] and [[@kathakali|Kathakali]] still train to show each one with the eyes, eyebrows and mouth. In 2015, the Pixar film Inside Out turned five emotions into cartoon characters. Paul Ekman and another scientist, Dacher Keltner, advised the [[@animation-studios|animation studio]] on the science.

It's easy to think some feelings are good and others are bad. But every emotion does something useful. Anger can tell you something is unfair. Fear keeps you careful near traffic. Sadness shows you what you care about. Feelings become a problem mainly when they're very strong for a long time, or when they push us to hurt ourselves or others.

Putting a feeling into words can help it settle. Talking to a friend, a parent or a teacher about how you feel isn't a sign of weakness. It's one of the best ways people have found to understand their own minds.

text: Puberty is the time when a child's body turns into an adult's. It usually starts between about 8 and 13 in girls and 9 and 14 in boys, and lasts a few years. Everyone's timing is different, and early or late are both usually normal.

It begins in [[@brain-works|the brain]]. A small part called the hypothalamus sends a signal to the pituitary [[gland|gland]] just below it. The pituitary then releases [[hormone|hormones]] into the blood. These tell the ovaries in girls to make more oestrogen, and the testes in boys to make more testosterone. These [[@hormones|hormones]] travel around the body and set off the changes of puberty, from [[@body-growth-spurts|a growth spurt]] to [[@body-voice-change|a deeper voice]].

st.reveal: Puberty begins when the hypothalamus, a small part of the brain, starts sending a signal to the pituitary gland just below it. The pituitary then sends hormones through the blood that tell the rest of the body to start changing.

Some changes happen to almost everyone. You [[@growing-taller|grow taller]], often very fast for a year or two. [[@hair-grow|Hair]] starts to grow under your arms and in other new places. The [[@sweat|sweat]] glands in your armpits wake up, so sweat starts to smell, and washing every day becomes more important.

Your [[@skin|skin]] makes more oil, which can block tiny pores and cause spots. Feet often grow before the rest of the body catches up, so for a while shoes get too small very fast. Many people feel clumsy during a growth spurt, because their brain is still getting used to longer arms and legs.

sec.h: Earlier than it used to be
sec.t: Puberty seems to start earlier now than it did long ago. In Europe in the 1800s, many girls had their first period at around 16 or 17. Today, in India, the USA and many other countries, the average is closer to 12 or 13. Doctors think better food and health play a big part, because the body needs enough energy stores before puberty can begin. Scientists are also studying whether other things, such as body weight and chemicals in the environment, play a part.

Puberty isn't only about the body. The brain is changing too. Through the teenage years it trims away connections it doesn't use and strengthens the ones it does, like a gardener pruning a hedge. The front part of the brain, which helps with planning and self-control, is among the last to finish, in the mid-twenties.

Hormones and a busy, rebuilding brain can make [[@emotions|feelings]] stronger and moods change faster. Teenagers also tend to feel sleepy later at night. All of this is normal. Bodies change at different speeds, and comparing yourself with friends can be confusing. Talking to a parent, a trusted adult or a doctor helps. Every adult you know has been through it.

text: Charles Babbage was an English mathematician and inventor, born in 1791. He designed two great calculating machines made of brass [[@gears|gears]], wheels and [[@lever-lift|levers]].

The first, the Difference Engine, would calculate mathematical tables automatically. The second, the Analytical Engine, was far more ambitious. It could be programmed with punched cards, had a memory and a separate unit to do calculations, and could make decisions based on its results. Those are the key parts of a modern computer.
Babbage never finished either machine. But because of these designs, he is often called the father of the computer.

st.prompt: In 1991, the Science Museum in London built Babbage's Difference Engine No. 2 using only his plans and the kind of precision possible in his day. What happened?

options.t: It worked, calculating correctly to 31 digits
It worked only after adding an electric motor

st.reveal: The finished calculating section, made of about 4,000 parts, worked as Babbage intended. It proved that his design was sound and that the engineering of his time could have built it, given enough money and patience.

d.try: Make a "difference table" like Babbage's engine. Write the square numbers 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 in a row. Underneath, write the differences between them (3, 5, 7, 9), then the differences between those (2, 2, 2). Now use only adding to extend the squares as far as you can. Babbage's engine did this with gears.
myth: Babbage's machines could never have worked with the technology of the 1800s.

The Science Museum built his Difference Engine No. 2 to his drawings, using tolerances achievable in his time, and it works. His projects stalled mainly because of money, arguments and his habit of redesigning, not because the ideas were impossible.

sec.t:
In Babbage's time, engineers, sailors and bankers relied on printed books of numbers: tables of logarithms, [[@tides|tides]] and star positions. These were worked out by hand by [[@moon-race-women|human computers]], then copied and typeset. Mistakes crept in at every step, and a wrong number in a ship's [[navigation|navigation]] table could wreck a ship.

In 1821, while checking tables with his friend the [[astronomer|astronomer]] John Herschel, Babbage found error after error. He is reported to have wished the calculations could be done by steam. That idea, a machine that never makes careless mistakes, drove the rest of his life.

Babbage's first design used a clever trick called the method of differences. Many tables, such as squares or [[@multiplication-tables|times tables]], can be built using only addition, if you start with the right differences. Adding is easy for gears.

The British government gave him money, and his engineer Joseph Clement began building it in the 1820s. In 1832, a small section was assembled and worked perfectly. But Babbage and Clement fell out over costs, and the government eventually stopped paying. Only a fraction of the machine was ever built in his lifetime.

Babbage had many interests. He held the same professorship of mathematics at Cambridge that [[@newton-life|Isaac Newton]] once held. He wrote about railways, [[@lighthouses|lighthouses]], codebreaking and factories, and is often credited with inventing the cowcatcher, a frame on the front of trains that pushes obstacles off the track.

He was also famously grumpy. He campaigned for years against the street musicians and organ grinders outside his house in [[@london|London]], whose noise, he said, ruined his concentration. They sometimes played under his window on purpose.

In 1991, the 200th anniversary of Babbage's birth, the Science Museum in London finished building his Difference Engine No. 2, a later and simpler design, using his original drawings. Its calculating section has about 4,000 parts and is turned by a hand crank. It worked. A printer, also designed by Babbage, was added in 2002, and together they weigh about 5 tonnes.

A second copy was made for the Computer History Museum in California. The Analytical Engine has never been built, though a project in Britain called Plan 28 has been studying his drawings in the hope of one day building it.

text: Albert Einstein showed that space and time are not fixed. They can stretch and shrink depending on how fast you move and how strong [[@gravity-fall|gravity]] is. This is his theory of relativity. He also showed that mass and energy are two forms of the same thing, written as E = mc², and that light travels in tiny packets of energy.
These ideas sound strange, but you use them every day. Phone [[navigation|navigation]], [[@solar-panels|solar panels]] and camera [[sensor|sensors]] all depend on physics Einstein helped discover.

st.prompt: Einstein won the Nobel Prize in Physics. Which discovery was it actually awarded for?

options.t: Explaining how light knocks electrons out of metal

st.reveal: The prize was for explaining the photoelectric effect, the idea that light comes in tiny packets of energy. It is the basis of solar panels and camera sensors. In 1921, relativity was still too new and too argued-over for the Nobel committee.

src.Isaacson W. (2007) Einstein: His Life and Universe. Simon & Schuster.

d.try: Stretch an old bedsheet tight with three or four people holding the edges. Put a heavy ball, like a melon or a cricket ball, in the middle. Now roll a marble across the sheet. It curves around the dip. Einstein said gravity works a bit like this, with heavy objects bending space itself.
myth: Einstein failed maths at school.

He was excellent at maths and had taught himself calculus by about the age of 15. He did fail the general section of a university entrance exam when he was 16, two years younger than most applicants, which may be where the story began.

sec.t:
Einstein was born in Ulm, Germany, in 1879. He did well in maths and science but disliked strict schools that made pupils memorise. After university in Zurich he could not find a teaching job, so in 1902 he became a clerk at the patent office in [[@switzerland|Bern, Switzerland]], checking other people's inventions.

In his spare time he thought about physics. In 1905, at 26, he published four papers. One explained the photoelectric effect. Another gave strong evidence that [[atom|atoms]] really exist by explaining how tiny grains jiggle in water. The third set out special relativity. The fourth, only three pages long, introduced E = mc².

sec.h: The eclipse that made him famous
sec.t:
General relativity predicted that the Sun's gravity would bend starlight passing near it. In 1919, British teams led by Arthur Eddington photographed stars during a total solar [[eclipse|eclipse]], from Brazil and an island off West Africa. The stars appeared slightly shifted, as Einstein had said. [[@newspapers|Newspapers]] around the world made him a celebrity overnight.

His theory also predicted [[@black-holes|black holes]] and ripples in space called gravitational waves. Scientists first detected those waves in 2015, a century later. It added to rather than replaced the work of [[@newton-life|Isaac Newton]], whose laws still work well for everyday speeds.

In 1924, a young physicist in Dhaka, Satyendra Nath Bose, sent Einstein a paper on how particles of light can be counted. Einstein was so impressed that he translated it into German himself and got it published. Their combined ideas are called Bose–Einstein [[statistics|statistics]], and one whole family of particles is called bosons, after Bose.

Einstein also met the poet [[@tagore|Rabindranath Tagore]] near Berlin in 1930. Their conversation about whether truth exists without humans was printed and is still read today.

Einstein was Jewish, and when the [[@holocaust|Nazis took power]] in 1933 he left Germany for the United States. He worked at Princeton until his death in 1955. In 1939 he signed a letter warning President Roosevelt that Germany might build an atomic bomb. He did not work on the American bomb himself, and later said he regretted signing the letter. He spent his last years speaking out for peace.

text: A robot is a machine that can sense the world around it, decide what to do, and then move to do it. Engineers call this "sense, think, act".

To sense, a robot uses [[sensor|sensors]]: cameras, microphones, touch pads, or beams of light that measure distance. To think, it uses a computer running a [[@programming|program]], a set of instructions written by people. To act, it uses motors that turn wheels, bend [[@joints|joints]] or squeeze grippers. Take away any one of the three and you have something simpler: a camera, a computer or a toy car.

st.prompt: Which kind of robot is there the most of in the world today?
st.reveal: Factories use millions of robot arms to weld, paint, lift and pack. Robots that look like people get lots of attention, but there are only a few of them, and most are still being tested.

d.try: Play "robot and programmer" with a friend. You are the programmer and must get your robot from one side of a room to a chair using only exact commands like "step forward" or "turn left". Your robot must do exactly what you say, nothing more. You will quickly see why real programs need to be so precise.
myth: Robots think and feel the way people do, like in the films.
Today's robots follow programs written by people. Some use artificial intelligence to recognise objects or plan a path, but none of them understand the world or have feelings the way you do.

sec.t:
The first robot to work in a factory was called Unimate. In 1961 it started lifting hot pieces of metal at a General Motors car plant in New Jersey, a job that was dangerous for people. It was basically a strong arm that repeated the same movements again and again.

Most robots today are still arms like that. In a modern car factory, rows of them weld the body together in showers of sparks, faster and steadier than any person. They don't need lunch breaks. But they are also not very clever. Move the car a few centimetres out of place, and an old-style robot arm will weld thin air.

Some robots go where people can't. [[@tech-robots-space|NASA's rovers]] have driven across Mars for years, steered by teams on Earth. Radio messages take several minutes to reach Mars, so the [[rover|rovers]] must handle some decisions on their own, like stopping before a rock.

India has a robot on the Moon too. In August 2023, Chandrayaan-3 landed near the [[@moon-water|Moon's south pole]] and released the [[@chandrayaan|Pragyan rover]]. It was about the size of a large suitcase. Over roughly ten days it rolled about 100 metres and tested the soil for [[element|elements]] such as sulphur.

sec.h: Why most robots don't look like us
sec.t:
In films, robots usually have two arms, two legs and a face. Real engineers build whatever shape suits the job. A robot that cleans a swimming pool looks like a small tank. One that operates inside the body is a set of thin arms that [[@robots-surgery|a surgeon controls from a console]].

Walking on two legs, it turns out, is extremely hard. You balance without thinking, but a machine must correct its weight many times every second or topple over. A few companies are now testing human-shaped robots for warehouses. Even so, the humble wheel is still the robot's best friend.

Hands are another puzzle. Picking up an egg without crushing it, or a sock without dropping it, needs a delicate sense of touch. Your fingertips have thousands of [[@nervous-system|nerve endings]]. Robot grippers are only starting to catch up, which is why [[@life-chores-world|folding laundry]] is still harder for a robot than welding a car.

text: Benjamin Franklin was an American printer, writer, scientist, inventor and statesman who lived from 1706 to 1790. He is one of the Founding Fathers of the United States, the group of leaders who broke away from Britain and set up the new country.

He showed that lightning is a form of electricity, and invented the lightning rod to protect buildings. He also invented bifocal glasses and a better wood stove, started a public library and a fire company, and helped write and sign the Declaration of Independence and the US Constitution. His face is on the $100 note.

st.prompt: In Franklin's kite experiment, what showed that the storm cloud carried electricity?

options.t: A spark jumped from a metal key on the string to his knuckle
The kite caught fire in the sky
The kite string glowed bright blue

st.reveal: Franklin wrote that the threads on the wet string stood up and a spark jumped from a key tied near the bottom. He was lucky. A direct lightning strike would have killed him. In 1753, a scientist in Russia, Georg Richmann, was killed while trying a similar experiment.

If it had been, he would almost certainly have died. Franklin said the kite picked up electric charge from the storm cloud, enough to make a small spark, but not a full lightning bolt.

sec.t:
Franklin was born in Boston, the 15th of 17 children of a soap and candle maker. His family could afford only two years of school. At 12, he became an apprentice to his older brother, a printer. He read every book he could borrow.

At 17, he ran away to Philadelphia with almost no money. He worked hard, set up his own print shop and became rich. His yearly almanac, *Poor Richard's Almanack*, was full of weather predictions, jokes and sayings like "Early to bed and early to rise, makes a man healthy, wealthy, and wise". It sold thousands of copies a year.

In the 1740s, scientists in Europe and America were excited about [[@static-electricity|static electricity]], making sparks with glass tubes and jars. Franklin noticed that sparks looked and crackled like tiny lightning. He wondered whether lightning was the same thing.

In June 1752, according to his own account, he flew a silk kite in a thunderstorm in Philadelphia, with a metal key tied to the string. When he moved his knuckle near the key, a spark jumped. He took it as proof. Some historians think the details were tidied up later, but scientists in France had already proved the same idea a month earlier, using one of his designs.

He then invented the [[@lightning-rods|lightning rod]], a pointed metal rod on a roof connected by a wire to the ground. It gives lightning a safe path, protecting the house. Lightning rods are still used on buildings, including temples and towers in India.

{{story:static-electricity}}

Franklin's mind never stopped. As he aged and needed two pairs of glasses, one for reading and one for distance, he cut the lenses in half and put them into one frame. These were bifocals. He designed the Franklin stove, which heated rooms better and used less wood. He also mapped the Gulf Stream, a warm ocean current in the Atlantic.

He started one of the first lending libraries in America, a volunteer fire company and a hospital in Philadelphia. He also helped found what became the University of Pennsylvania.

Franklin began as a loyal British subject but came to believe the colonies should be free. In 1776, he helped [[@thomas-jefferson|Thomas Jefferson]] edit the Declaration of Independence and signed it. During the [[@american-revolution|American Revolution]], he went to France and persuaded the French king to send money, soldiers and ships. Without that help, the Americans might have lost.

In 1787, at 81, he was the oldest delegate at the convention that wrote the US Constitution.

For much of his life, Franklin owned enslaved people and printed advertisements for slave sales in his newspaper. Over time, his views changed. In his last years he became president of the Pennsylvania Abolition Society, and in 1790 he asked Congress to end slavery. Congress refused. He died two months later, aged 84. About 20,000 people attended his funeral, the largest Philadelphia had seen.

text: The Black Death was a massive outbreak of plague that swept across Asia, the Middle East, North Africa and Europe in the mid-1300s. In Europe, the worst years were 1347 to 1351. Historians estimate it killed between a third and half of Europe's people, perhaps 25 million or more.

Plague is caused by a [[bacteria|bacterium]] called *Yersinia pestis*. It usually lives in rodents such as rats and is spread by their fleas. When infected fleas bite people, they can pass on the disease. In some cases it also spreads directly from person to person through coughing. Without medicine, most people who caught it died within days.

st.prompt: Where does the word "quarantine" come from?

st.reveal: In the 1300s, the port of Ragusa (today's Dubrovnik) made ships from plague areas wait in isolation before landing, at first for 30 days. Later, 40 days became the rule, quaranta giorni in Italian, which gave us "quarantine".

n.certNote: Scientists have confirmed the germ that caused the Black Death by finding its DNA in skeletons. How many people died is an estimate, usually between a third and a half of Europe's population, and experts still debate exactly how it spread so quickly.

sec.t:
The plague probably began in Central Asia. In 2022, scientists studied skeletons from two old cemeteries in the Chüy Valley of Kyrgyzstan, not far from Lake Issyk-Kul, where gravestones from 1338 and 1339 mention a deadly illness. They found plague DNA in the teeth, matching the strain that later spread west.

The disease travelled along trade routes, including the [[@silk-road|Silk Road]], carried by merchants, soldiers and their animals. By 1346 it had reached the Black Sea. In October 1347, ships from there arrived in Messina, in Sicily. Within months it was in Italy, France and Spain, and by 1349 it had reached England and Norway.

People did notice that the disease moved with travellers. In 1377, the port of Ragusa, now Dubrovnik in Croatia, ordered ships and travellers from plague areas to wait 30 days before entering the city. Venice and other cities later made it 40 days, *quaranta giorni* in Italian. That is where the word "[[quarantine|quarantine]]" comes from.

These were some of the first [[@public-health|public health]] rules of their kind. Cities also appointed health officers and set up special hospitals. Quarantine is still used today, for example during the COVID-19 [[pandemic|pandemic]].

With so many people dead, there were not enough workers to farm the land. In parts of Europe, surviving peasants could demand higher wages and more freedom. When rulers tried to stop this, anger boiled over in revolts such as the Peasants' Revolt in England in 1381.

Plague kept returning to Europe every few years for centuries. It also struck the Middle East, North Africa and parts of Asia, though records from those places are less complete.

Plague has not disappeared. It still lives in wild rodents in parts of Africa, Asia and the Americas. Madagascar and the Democratic Republic of the Congo report the most cases. In the western United States, a handful of people catch it each year, usually from wild rodents or their fleas. India had an outbreak in Surat in 1994.

The difference is that plague can now be cured. [[@antibiotics|Antibiotics]], discovered in the 20th century, kill the bacterium if treatment starts early. A disease that once emptied whole villages can now be treated in a hospital in about a week or two.

text: It depends on what you call a university. If you mean a big place where students lived and studied many subjects with expert teachers, one of the earliest was Nalanda, in what is now Bihar, India. It began in the 5th century CE and ran for about 700 years.

If you mean the oldest one still working today, the usual answer is al-Qarawiyyin in Fez, Morocco, founded in 859. And if you mean the first place to call itself a university, with degrees, students' groups and the word *universitas*, that was Bologna in Italy, from 1088. All three answers are true in their own way.

They paid a large fee in gold
Anyone could walk in and attend

st.reveal: The Chinese traveller Xuanzang wrote that learned men at the gate questioned anyone who wanted to enter. He said many failed and went home. It was one of the world's earliest entrance exams.

n.certNote: There is no single answer. Nalanda and Takshashila were great centres of learning long before Europe's universities. Al-Qarawiyyin in Morocco, founded in 859, is often called the oldest still running. Bologna, from 1088, was the first to call itself a "university" in the European sense.

d.try: Hold a mini "Nalanda debate" at home or in class. Pick a simple question, such as "Is it better to be a morning person or a night person?" One side argues yes, the other no, each with three reasons. Swap sides halfway through. Nalanda students practised debating like this.
myth: Universities were invented in medieval Europe.

The word "university" comes from Europe, but large centres of higher learning existed much earlier in India, and in the Islamic world institutions like al-Qarawiyyin and al-Azhar began before Europe's first universities.

sec.t:
Nalanda started as a Buddhist [[monastery|monastery]] and grew under the [[@gupta-golden-age|Gupta kings]] and later rulers. At its height it had huge brick buildings, temples, lecture halls, gardens, ponds and rooms for thousands of monks. Its library was said to fill three buildings, one of them nine storeys tall, though that detail comes from later Tibetan tradition.

Students studied Buddhist teachings, but also grammar, logic, medicine, mathematics and astronomy. Debate was a big part of learning. A student had to defend ideas against sharp questions in front of others.

The Chinese monk Xuanzang studied there in the 600s. He walked from China, across deserts and the Himalayas, and stayed for years. He wrote that around 10,000 monks and students lived there, though some historians think that number is too high. Others came from Korea, Tibet, Central Asia and Southeast Asia. Another Chinese monk, Yijing, studied at Nalanda later in the same century and copied hundreds of texts to take home.

{{story:nalanda}}

Even earlier, there was Takshashila, near today's Islamabad in Pakistan. By around 500 BCE, it was famous for its teachers. Tradition links it to the grammarian Panini, the physician Jivaka and the political thinker [[@chanakya|Chanakya]].

But Takshashila was more like a town full of independent teachers than one organised institution. Students went to live with a teacher of their choice. That is why many historians save the word "university" for Nalanda instead.

sec.h: A woman founds a school in Fez
sec.t:
In 859, a wealthy woman named Fatima al-Fihri, whose family had moved to Fez from Tunisia, used her inheritance to build a mosque in the city. It grew into a great centre of learning, with teachers of religion, law, grammar, astronomy and medicine. Scholars travelled across North Africa, Spain and beyond to study there.

Today it is the University of al-Qarawiyyin. Guinness World Records lists it as the oldest existing educational institution in the world. Its library, one of the oldest anywhere, still holds handwritten books more than 1,000 years old.

In Europe, the University of Bologna began around 1088. Students, many of them adults studying law, banded together into groups to hire teachers and protect themselves. Their group was called a *universitas*, and that is where the word "university" comes from.

Paris and Oxford followed in the 1100s. The oldest university in the USA, Harvard, was founded in 1636. India's first modern universities, in Calcutta, Bombay and Madras, opened in 1857.

Around 1200, Nalanda was attacked and burned. Many accounts blame the army of Bakhtiyar Khalji, though historians still discuss exactly what happened. The monks scattered, and the great library was lost. Its ruins were rediscovered in the 1800s and became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016.

A new Nalanda University now stands nearby. Its campus opened in 2024, with students from many countries, just as in Xuanzang's day. Along with [[@bodh-gaya|Bodh Gaya]] and the other old Buddhist sites of Bihar, it draws visitors from across Asia who come to see where some of the world's first great universities began.

text: Ancient people used everything from simple holes and pots to surprisingly clever toilets with running water. About 4,500 years ago, in Indus Valley cities like Mohenjo-daro and Harappa, many houses had a toilet connected to brick drains under the streets. The Romans built public toilets where dozens of people sat side by side, with water flowing below to carry waste away.

Most people in history, though, used chamber pots, pits, fields or rivers. Toilets with pipes and drains were a luxury for cities and the rich. Some of these ancient systems were better than what many European towns had a thousand years later.

st.prompt: In Roman public toilets, what did people probably use instead of toilet paper?

options.t: A sea sponge on a stick, rinsed in water

st.reveal: Romans had no paper. Many historians think they used a tersorium, a sponge fixed to a stick and rinsed in a channel of water at their feet. Some experts think it was for cleaning the toilets instead, which is why the question is still argued.

n.certNote: Archaeologists can see ancient toilet seats and drains clearly. How some things were used, such as the Roman sponge on a stick, is still debated.

sec.t:
The cities of the Indus Valley, in today's India and Pakistan, were planned with great care for drains. Houses in Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Lothal and Dholavira often had a bathing area and a toilet. Waste water flowed through clay pipes into covered brick drains along the streets.

The drains had removable covers so workers could clean them. Some houses even had seats made of brick over a pot or a chute. [[archaeologist|Archaeologists]] think few ancient cities managed waste this well. You can explore how these cities were laid out in [[@indus-cities|Indus Valley cities]].

sec.h: A village in the far north
sec.t:
On the island of Orkney, off the north of Scotland, lies Skara Brae, a stone village about 5,000 years old. Its houses had drains built under the floors. Some small side rooms may have been toilets, flushed by a nearby stream.

That makes Skara Brae older than the Egyptian pyramids. Its people built stone beds and shelves too, all still standing today.

In 2023, archaeologists working at the ruins of an ancient palace near Xi'an, in China, found a toilet with a pipe running outside. It was about 2,400 years old. They believe servants poured water into it to flush it away, making it one of the oldest known flushing toilets.

Elsewhere in ancient China, some toilets sat above pig pens, and the pigs ate the waste. Clay models of these "pig toilets" were placed in tombs.

[[medieval|Medieval]] castles in Europe had small toilet rooms called garderobes, built into the outer wall. Waste dropped straight down the side of the castle, often into the moat. Most townspeople used chamber pots and emptied them into the street.

In 1596, an English courtier named Sir John Harington built a flushing toilet for his godmother, Queen Elizabeth I. It didn't catch on. Flush toilets became common only in the late 1800s, once cities built proper sewers.

Clean toilets save lives by keeping germs out of drinking water. Yet in 2022, about 3.5 billion people still lacked a safely managed toilet. India's Swachh Bharat Mission, launched in 2014, built more than 100 million household toilets. The United Nations marks World Toilet Day on 19 November.

From Indus drains to the [[@toilets-sewers|sewers under your street]], the problem has always been the same. Even astronauts have to solve it.

text: The Brahmaputra is one of Asia's great rivers. It rises in Tibet, near Mount Kailash, flows east across the high Tibetan plateau for over 1,000 km, then makes a sharp turn and cuts south through the Himalaya into India. It crosses Arunachal Pradesh and Assam, enters Bangladesh, and joins the Ganga before reaching the Bay of Bengal.

It is special for its size, its power and its moods. In Assam it can be several kilometres wide, braided into many channels around shifting sandbanks. It carries huge amounts of water and silt, floods most years, and has shaped the life, culture and wildlife of the whole valley.

st.prompt: In Assam, the Brahmaputra splits into many channels around sandbanks that shift every year. What is this kind of river called?
st.reveal: A braided river carries so much sand and silt that it keeps dropping it in bars and islands, then flowing around them in many criss-crossing channels, like strands in a plait. The Brahmaputra is one of the largest braided rivers in the world.
