d.try: See how a braided river forms. In a long tray, make a gentle slope of sand mixed with a little soil. Pour water slowly from the top for a few minutes, adding a spoonful of extra sand to the water now and then. Watch channels split around little sandbanks and join again.
myth: All of India's big rivers are named after goddesses.

The Brahmaputra's name means "son of Brahma", one of very few big Indian rivers given a male name. In Assam it is also called the Luit. The Son, in central India, is another river traditionally seen as male.
facts: near Mount Kailash and Lake Manasarovar, in Tibet
Yarlung Tsangpo (Tibet), Siang (Arunachal Pradesh), Brahmaputra (Assam), Jamuna (Bangladesh)

sec.t:
In Tibet the river is called the Yarlung Tsangpo. It runs at more than 3,000 metres above sea level, among the highest major rivers on Earth. Near a mountain called Namcha Barwa it bends in a giant U-turn and plunges through the Yarlung Tsangpo Grand Canyon, one of the deepest gorges in the world.

When it enters Arunachal Pradesh, it is called the Siang. Joined by the Dibang and the Lohit, it becomes the Brahmaputra in Assam. In Bangladesh it takes the name Jamuna, and after meeting the Ganga (there called the Padma), it flows on to the sea. It ends in the same delta as the [[@ganga-journey|Ganga]], with its huge mangrove forests.

The Brahmaputra drains young, steep mountains that are still rising and crumbling. Heavy [[monsoon|monsoon]] rains wash rock and soil into it, so it carries one of the biggest loads of silt of any river. Where the land flattens in Assam, the river slows and drops sand, building bars and islands. Then it flows around them in many channels.

The river keeps changing course. Villages that stood on a bank one year can be in the water the next. That makes the river hard to bridge. The Bogibeel Bridge near Dibrugarh, opened in 2018, carries both a road and a railway about 4.9 km across it. Floods come almost every monsoon, damaging homes and farms. But they also spread fresh silt over the fields, making them [[fertile|fertile]], and feed the [[wetland|wetlands]] and grasslands along the river.

Hundreds of sandy islands, called *chars* or *chaporis*, dot the river. The biggest is [[@majuli|Majuli]], home to about 1.7 lakh people (2011 Census). It is famous for its *satras*, [[monastery|monasteries]] started in the tradition of the saint Srimanta Sankardeva in the 1500s, where monks keep alive dance, drama and mask-making.

Majuli is in danger. As the river wears away its banks, the island has shrunk. It covered roughly 1,250 square km in the early 1900s, and between about 350 and 500 today, depending on how it is measured. Walls and other protection works are trying to slow the loss.

For people in Assam, the Brahmaputra is more than water. The singer Bhupen Hazarika grew up near its banks. In his song "Bistirno Parore", he asks the great river why it flows on silently while people suffer on its shores. A Hindi version, "Ganga Behti Ho Kyun", asks the same of the Ganga. In 2017, India opened a 9 km bridge from Dhola to Sadiya, over a [[tributary|tributary]] of the Brahmaputra. It was then the country's longest river bridge, and it was named after him.

text: A continent is one of Earth's very large land masses. Schools in India and the USA usually teach seven: Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe and Australia.
Asia is the biggest, with about 30% of all the land on Earth and more than half its people. Australia is the smallest. Antarctica is the coldest and the only one with no permanent population.

The number seven is partly a choice. Europe and Asia are really one connected land mass, and North and South America are joined too. So in some countries, children learn six continents, or even five. The land doesn't change, only the way people group it.

st.prompt: Which continent has no countries of its own and no permanent residents?
st.reveal: Antarctica is shared under a treaty signed in 1959, which says it must be used only for peaceful purposes and science. Scientists from many countries, including India, live at research stations there, but only for months at a time.

src: National Geographic Society, Continent.
Encyclopaedia Britannica, Continent.
n.certNote: Geologists agree on the land masses, but how many continents there are is a matter of custom. Schools in India and the USA teach seven, while many in Latin America and Europe teach six.

d.try: Trace the continents from an atlas onto a sheet of paper and tear them out roughly with your fingers. Try fitting the east coast of South America against the west coast of Africa. Scientists noticed this jigsaw fit hundreds of years ago, and it was one of the first clues that continents move.
myth: Africa is a country.
Africa is a continent with 54 countries, more than any other continent. It is home to over a thousand languages and is large enough to fit India, China and the USA inside it at once.
facts: Number taught in India and the USA

sec.t:
Look at a globe and you will see no gap between Europe and Asia. The usual dividing line runs along the Ural Mountains in [[@russia|Russia]], down to the Caspian Sea. That line was chosen by geographers centuries ago, partly for cultural reasons.

In much of Latin America and in countries like Spain, students learn that America is a single continent. The five Olympic rings, designed in 1913, were said to stand for the five inhabited continents, with the Americas counted as one.

India once sat far south, near Africa, Antarctica and Australia. When the giant southern land broke apart, the Indian plate drifted north across the ocean, faster than most plates.

About 5 crore years ago, it crashed into Asia. The collision crumpled the land and began pushing up the [[@himalaya-form|Himalaya]], which are still rising by a few millimetres a year. That is why geographers often call India a [[subcontinent|subcontinent]].

[[@antarctica|Antarctica]] is bigger than India and China combined. Almost all of it lies under ice, in places more than 4 km thick. In 1959, twelve countries signed the Antarctic Treaty, which keeps the continent for peace and science. Many more countries have signed since.

India runs [[@antarctica-stations|research stations]] there, called Maitri and Bharati. Scientists study ice, weather and ancient air trapped in bubbles.

Because continents drifted apart long ago, each has its own animals. Kangaroos and koalas live wild only in [[@australia|Australia]], which has been cut off from other land for tens of millions of years. Lions and giraffes roam Africa. Llamas come from South America, and the bald eagle soars over North America.

People spread across the continents too. Scientists think modern humans first lived in Africa and then moved out, reaching Asia, Australia, Europe and finally the Americas. They probably reached the Americas over land that joined Siberia and [[@alaska|Alaska]] during the last Ice Age.

Some [[geologist|geologists]] argue there is an eighth continent, Zealandia, around [[@new-zealand|New Zealand]]. About 94% of it is under the sea. In 2017, a team of scientists published a paper arguing it should count. Not everyone agrees, which shows that even continents can be up for debate.

text: The Sahara covers about 9.2 million square kilometres of North Africa. That is nearly as big as the whole of the United States, and almost three times the size of India. It stretches about 4,800 km from the Atlantic coast in the west to the Red Sea in the east, which is further than the whole length of India from Kashmir to Kanyakumari.

Parts of more than ten countries lie in it, including Egypt, Libya, Algeria, [[@morocco|Morocco]], Mali, Niger, Chad and Sudan. It is the largest hot desert on Earth. In some places, years can pass without a single shower of rain. Yet the Sahara is not empty. Millions of people live in its towns and [[oasis|oases]], along with foxes, lizards, beetles and hardy plants that can wait out long [[@droughts|droughts]].

st.prompt: When you picture the Sahara, you probably picture sand dunes. How much of it is actually dunes?
st.reveal: Most of the Sahara is bare rocky plateau, gravel plains, dry valleys and mountains. The great seas of sand, called ergs, are spectacular but cover only around a quarter of it.

d.try: Spread a thin layer of flour or fine sand on a tray. Blow gently across it through a straw from one side and watch ripples and little dunes form. Notice which side of each ripple is steep and which is gentle.
myth: The Sahara is the biggest desert in the world.
It is the biggest hot desert. Antarctica and the Arctic count as deserts too, because so little snow or rain falls there, and both are larger than the Sahara.

sec.t:
When people think of the Sahara, they think of golden dunes. Some dunes really are huge, taller than a 50-storey building. Wind piles them up and slowly pushes them across the land, grain by grain, as you can read in [[@deserts-sand|desert sand]].

But most of the Sahara is not sand. It is rocky plateaus, plains of gravel, dry riverbeds and mountains. The Tibesti Mountains in Chad rise to about 3,400 m and sometimes get snow. Temperatures swing hard, too. A day can reach well over 40 °C, and the clear night sky lets the heat escape so fast that it can drop close to freezing before dawn.

The Sahara has not always been a desert. Between roughly 11,000 and 5,000 years ago, [[@monsoon|the monsoon]] rains reached much further north. Grasslands and lakes spread across the region. Hippos, crocodiles, giraffes and elephants lived there, and so did people, who herded cattle and fished.

They left paintings and carvings on rocks, showing cattle, hunters and even people who appear to be swimming. The change happened because Earth's [[orbit|orbit]] wobbles slowly over thousands of years, shifting where the rain falls. As the rains moved south, the lakes dried up and people moved away, many towards the Nile.

Every year, strong winds lift enormous amounts of Saharan dust high into the air. NASA satellites have tracked these clouds as they cross the Atlantic Ocean. Some of the dust falls on the Caribbean and the southern United States, turning sunsets hazy.

Some of it lands on the [[@brazil-amazon|Amazon rainforest]]. The dust carries phosphorus, a [[nutrient|nutrient]] that the Amazon's rain-soaked soil keeps losing. So in a strange way, the biggest hot desert on Earth helps feed the biggest rainforest. The Nile, meanwhile, flows along the Sahara's eastern edge, a ribbon of green fields between two walls of sand.

text: A cake is mostly bubbles. When you stir batter, you trap air in it. Then a raising agent, usually baking powder or baking soda, makes extra bubbles of [[carbon-dioxide|carbon dioxide]] gas.

In a hot oven, every bubble swells as the gas inside expands, and water turns into steam that pushes outwards too. The batter puffs up. Then the heat sets the eggs and flour into a firm, spongy wall around each bubble, so the cake stays tall after it cools. A good cake is really a frozen foam.

st.prompt: Which gas makes most cakes and breads rise?
st.reveal: Baking soda, baking powder and yeast all give off carbon dioxide, the same gas that makes the fizz in a cold drink. Heat in the oven makes those bubbles swell before the batter sets around them.

src: McGee H. (2004) On Food and Cooking. Scribner.
Encyclopaedia Britannica, baking powder.
Science History Institute, history of baking powder.

d.try: Put two spoons of baking soda inside a balloon. Pour a little vinegar into an empty plastic bottle, stretch the balloon over the neck, then lift it so the powder falls in. The gas that blows up the balloon is the same gas that lifts a cake.
myth: Baking soda and baking powder are the same thing.
Baking soda is pure sodium bicarbonate. It needs something sour, like curd or lemon juice, to make gas. Baking powder already contains a dry acid mixed in, so it only needs water and heat.
facts: Main gas in a rising cake

sec.t:
There are three main ways to get gas into dough or batter. The first is pure muscle. Beating butter and sugar together, or whisking eggs, folds in tiny air pockets.

The second is chemistry. Baking soda reacts with something sour, like [[@lassi-chaas|buttermilk]], curd or lemon, and fizzes out carbon dioxide. Baking powder mixes soda with a dry [[acid|acid]], so it fizzes as soon as it gets wet and again when it gets hot.

The third is biology. [[yeast|Yeast]] feeds on sugar in bread dough and breathes out carbon dioxide, slowly, over an hour or two. That [[@food-science-bread-rise|slow rise]] is a kind of [[@fermentation|fermentation]], and it adds flavour too.

Gas alone would just escape. To hold it, a cake needs walls that can stretch and then set. Wheat flour forms [[gluten|gluten]], a stretchy net of [[protein|proteins]], when it gets wet and mixed. Eggs add more protein, and flour [[starch|starch]] swells and thickens.

As the cake bakes, the walls stiffen. That is why a cake that comes out too early can sink in the middle: the bubbles cool and shrink before the walls are strong enough to hold them up. Bread has much more gluten than cake, which is why it is chewy and a cake crumbles.

For most of history, bread rose only with yeast or with a bit of old, sour dough saved from the last batch. In 1843 an English chemist called Alfred Bird made an early baking powder so that his wife, who could not eat yeast, could still enjoy raised bread. Chemists in the United States improved the recipe in the following decades, and cheap tins of baking powder changed home baking on both sides of the Atlantic.

Cakes behave differently at height. In Denver, a mile above the sea, or in Shimla, the air pressure is lower, so bubbles grow bigger and faster and can burst before the cake sets. Bakers in high places often use a little less baking powder and a slightly hotter oven. It is a neat reminder that a [[@bubbles-round|bubble]] is always fighting the air pressing on it from outside.

text: Chillies contain a chemical called [[capsaicin|capsaicin]]. In your mouth it attaches to tiny [[sensor|sensors]] on your [[@nervous-system|nerve endings]]. These sensors normally switch on when something is dangerously hot, above about 43 °C.

[[@food-science-spicy-milk|Capsaicin]] flips the same switch without any real heat. Your brain gets a message that says "burning", so your face goes red, your eyes water and your nose runs, as if you had bitten into something scorching. Nothing is actually being cooked. It is a very convincing false alarm.

st.prompt: Your mouth is on fire after a spicy curry. Which drink will cool it down best?

options.t: A glass of milk or lassi

st.reveal: Capsaicin, the hot chemical in chillies, mixes with fat but not with water. Milk contains fat and a protein called casein that help wash it away. That is why raita and lassi go so well with spicy food.

d.try: Ask an adult to cut a green capsicum and a green chilli in half lengthwise. Using a spoon, not your fingers, look for the pale ribs inside each one where the seeds attach. That is where most of the heat is stored. Wash your hands afterwards and keep them away from your eyes.
myth: The seeds are the hottest part of a chilli.
Most of the capsaicin is made in the pale ribs and pith inside the chilli, where the seeds are attached. Seeds taste hot mainly because they touch those ribs.

sec.t:
In 1912 an American chemist, Wilbur Scoville, invented a way to rank chillies. He [[dissolve|dissolved]] chilli extract in sugar water and asked tasters to say when they could no longer feel any heat. The more it had to be diluted, the hotter the chilli.

Today labs measure capsaicin with machines, but the results are still given in Scoville heat units. A capsicum scores zero. A jalapeño scores a few thousand. The bhut jolokia, or ghost pepper, scores over a million.

The bhut jolokia grows in Assam, Nagaland and Manipur in [[@northeast-india|Northeast India]]. In 2007 [[@world-records|Guinness World Records]] named it the hottest chilli in the world. Hotter chillies bred in the United States, such as the Carolina Reaper, have since taken the title.

In Nagaland, the bhut jolokia goes into chutneys and pork dishes. It has even been used in smoke bombs and fences to keep wild elephants away from fields.

It can be surprising, but India had no chillies until about 500 years ago. Chillies come from Central and South America. Portuguese traders brought them to [[@goa|Goa]] in the 1500s, and within a century they had spread across the [[subcontinent|subcontinent]].

Before that, Indian cooks got their heat from black pepper, ginger and long pepper. Chillies were cheap and easy to grow, so they quickly became part of everyday food. India is now the world's largest producer of dried chillies.

When your mouth is burning, water does not help much. Capsaicin is an oily chemical, and like oil on a plate, water slides right past it. Milk, curd and [[@lassi-chaas|lassi]] work better because their fat and [[protein|proteins]] help carry the capsaicin away.

That may be one reason so many spicy cuisines serve cooling foods on the side. India has raita and buttermilk, [[@mexico|Mexico]] has sour cream, and [[@thailand|Thailand]] has coconut milk. Sugar and starchy rice also help a little. The feeling fades by itself after a few minutes, as the nerve sensors calm down.

Capsaicin seems to protect chilli plants. [[mammal|Mammals]] that chew seeds, like mice, feel the burn and stay away. Birds swallow seeds whole and carry them far away in their droppings, and birds cannot feel capsaicin. Capsaicin also helps fight off some [[fungus|fungi]] that attack the fruit.

So humans are odd. We are mammals that eat chillies anyway, often on purpose. Some scientists think people enjoy the rush of a safe danger, like a scary ride, and the body's own pain-relief chemicals that follow.

text: India has a long and close relationship with sugar. Indians were the first to turn sugarcane juice into crystals, more than 1,500 years ago, so sweet things have been part of Indian life for a very long time. India also produces more milk than any other country, and milk is the base of [[@sweets-world|many sweets]].

But sweets in India are about more than taste. They mark happy moments. People hand out sweets when a baby is born, when exams are passed and when a new job begins. Sweets are offered to gods in temples and [[@festival-foods|shared at every festival]]. In many families, saying "muh meetha karo", sweeten your mouth, is part of celebrating good news.

st.prompt: Where does the name "gulab jamun" come from?

options.t: Rose-scented syrup (gulab) and a round dark fruit it looks like (jamun)
The name of the cook who first made it
A town called Gulab in Rajasthan

st.reveal: Gulab is the Persian word for rose, from the rose water in its syrup. Jamun is a small dark purple fruit, and fried gulab jamuns are about the same shape and colour.

d.try: Ask your family about the sweets they eat at festivals, birthdays and weddings. Make a table with three columns, for the occasion, the sweet and the main ingredient. Count how many sweets are made from milk. Compare with a friend from another state.
myth: Jalebi is an ancient Indian sweet.
Jalebi probably came from West Asia, where zalabiya was described in cookbooks over a thousand years ago. It reached India by around the 1400s and has been an Indian favourite ever since.

sec.t:
The word sugar itself comes from the Sanskrit *sharkara*, as you can read in [[@sugar|where sugar comes from]]. Jaggery and honey were used in sweets for centuries before refined sugar.

Many Indian sweets start with [[@milk|milk]]. Boiled slowly, milk thickens into khoa, which becomes peda, barfi and the base of [[@food-gulab-jamun|gulab jamun]]. Rice cooked in milk becomes kheer or payasam. Ghee adds richness to halwas and [[@food-laddoo|laddoos]] made from wheat, besan or semolina.

In Bengal and Odisha, sweet makers use chhena, fresh cheese curds made by splitting milk with [[acid|acid]]. Kneaded smooth, chhena becomes sandesh and [[@bengali-food|rasgulla]].

Rasgulla, soft white balls cooked in sugar syrup, is claimed by both West Bengal and Odisha. Odisha links it to an old tradition at the Jagannath temple in Puri. West Bengal credits a [[@kolkata|Kolkata]] sweet maker named Nobin Chandra Das in 1868. Each state now has a GI tag for its own version.

Some Indian sweets came from elsewhere. Gulab jamun is related to luqmat al-qadi, a Persian and Arab fried dough ball in syrup. [[@food-jalebi|Jalebi]] probably came from West Asian zalabiya. Halwa takes its name from an Arabic word for sweet.

India made each of them its own. Indian jalebi is crisp, orange and soaked in syrup, often eaten hot for breakfast with rabri in the north. Mysore pak, made from besan, sugar and lots of ghee, is often said to have been invented in the kitchen of the Mysore palace.

sec.h: The halwai and the silver leaf
sec.t:
A traditional sweet maker is called a halwai. Some sweet shops in old cities have been run by the same family for more than a hundred years. Sweets are often decorated with varq, sheets of edible silver so thin they flutter when you breathe on them.

In the USA, Indian sweet shops now sell barfi and jalebi in New Jersey, Houston and California, especially during Diwali. American children have their own sugar-filled festival, [[@halloween|Halloween]], which shows that sweets and celebrations go together almost everywhere.

Indian sweets are rich in sugar and fat, which taste wonderful but aren't meant for every meal. Sugar left on teeth feeds [[bacteria|bacteria]] that cause cavities, which you can read about in [[@sugar-teeth|sugar and teeth]]. That's why many families enjoy sweets mostly on special days, and why a single piece can feel like a celebration.
